message.content:
Los Angeles (Pacific Time) is normally **9 hours behind** Berlin (Central European Time).  
However, because the U.S. and Europe change their clocks on slightly different dates, there are short windows each year when the gap shrinks to **8 hours**:

| Period | U.S. DST | Europe DST | Time‑zone offset | Difference |
|--------|----------|------------|------------------|------------|
| Early March – mid‑March | **No** (UTC‑8) | **Yes** (UTC+1) | Berlin +1, Los Angeles –8 | 9 h |
| Mid‑March – late March | **Yes** (UTC‑7) | **No** (UTC+1) | Berlin +1, Los Angeles –7 | 8 h |
| Late March – late October | **Yes** (UTC‑7) | **Yes** (UTC+2) | Berlin +2, Los Angeles –7 | 9 h |
| Late October – early November | **No** (UTC‑8) | **Yes** (UTC+2) | Berlin +2, Los Angeles –8 | 8 h |
| Early November – end of year | **No** (UTC‑8) | **No** (UTC+1) | Berlin +1, Los Angeles –8 | 9 h |

So, unless you’re in one of those brief transition weeks, you can safely assume a 9‑hour difference. If you need the exact offset for a specific date, a quick online time‑zone converter or a world clock app will give you the precise answer.
